findings.finding: The equal-chord properties are required in reverse before either converse is taught.
findings.breakdown: Guided practice b requires equal perpendicular distances to imply equal chords; question 1e requires equal central angles to imply equal chords. The stated forward implications alone do not justify either conclusion.
findings.checked: p12-properties-top states only the forward implications, and both introductory examples use those directions. Earlier circle-feature and angle-identification teaching supplies neither converse. The perpendicular-bisector properties address a different relationship.
findings.assumptions: Triangle congruence is prior knowledge, but these converse circle properties are new content. Practice answers are not preceding instruction.

repair.proposal: Before p12-guided-block, add: “For chords in the same circle, these two properties also work in reverse: equal central angles imply equal chords, and equal perpendicular distances from the centre imply equal chords.”

findings.doneWhen: Both converse properties are explicitly available before their first application.

findings.finding: The opening does not rehearse distribution and linear-equation solving, although both are direct steps in the introductory secant and tangent examples.
findings.breakdown: Following the geometric product equation requires expanding a numerical bracket and isolating the unknown through several equivalent equations. Neither skill is rehearsed immediately beforehand.
findings.checked: p32-example-secants expands 8(x+8); p32-example-tangent expands 5(5+x). Both then solve linear equations. The preceding tangent teaching and supplied preceding exercise rehearse geometry rather than these algebraic operations.
findings.assumptions: Expansion and linear-equation solving are prior learning, consistent with the separate course booklets. Calculator availability does not replace these symbolic steps.

repair.proposal: Before p32-properties-block, add: “Expand: (a) 3(y+4), (b) 5(2+y). Solve: (c) 6y=21, (d) 4y+12=30, (e) 3(y+4)=27.” Answers: 3y+12; 10+5y; y=3.5; y=4.5; y=5.

findings.doneWhen: A short opening review checks distribution and linear-equation solving before the geometric product examples.

findings.finding: Six whole mixed-practice tasks repeat earlier guided tasks without an explicit instructional purpose for the exact repetition.
findings.breakdown: Each pair retains the same requested quantities, numerical givens and geometric relationships. Relabelling the task does not create a new application.
findings.checked: Compared all six pairs: p12-guided-a-content/p36-q1-a; p18-part-a/p36-q1-d; p18-part-b/p36-q1-e; p12-guided-b-content/p38-hh; p32-guided-a/p39-vv; p32-guided-b/p39-hhh. Their complete mathematical tasks match. The supplied instructions establish neither retrieval of these particular tasks nor comparison with earlier responses.
findings.assumptions: The specified duplicate-task exception applies. A mixed-practice heading alone does not explicitly justify unchanged copies.

repair.proposal: Remove the later copies p36-q1-a, p36-q1-d, p36-q1-e, p38-hh, p39-vv and p39-hhh.

findings.doneWhen: Each targeted whole task appears once, or its exact repetition has an explicit instructional purpose.

findings.finding: The cyclicity proofs require converse criteria that the preceding teaching never states.
findings.breakdown: Establishing supplementary opposite angles or an exterior angle equal to the opposite interior angle does not follow the stated direction of either cyclic-quadrilateral theorem. Students need a criterion permitting the conclusion that the quadrilateral is cyclic.
findings.checked: p25-definition identifies cyclic quadrilaterals by circumference membership. p25-opposite-angles and p25-exterior-angle give forward properties; the examples and guided questions apply those properties to quadrilaterals already known to be cyclic. Earlier angle and chord teaching supplies no converse cyclicity test.
findings.assumptions: Elementary angle sums and congruence are prior knowledge; converse cyclicity criteria are new circle-geometry content.

repair.proposal: Before p46-q6, add: “To prove that a quadrilateral is cyclic, it is enough to show that one pair of opposite interior angles sums to 180°. Equivalently, show that an exterior angle equals the opposite interior angle. These are converse tests of the earlier cyclic-quadrilateral properties.”

findings.doneWhen: Both questions have an explicitly taught criterion justifying their final cyclicity conclusion.

findings.finding: Extend the common-chord theorem by comparing centre separations on opposite sides and on the same side of the chord.
findings.breakdown: The task asks students to explain when perpendicular centre-to-chord distances are added or subtracted.
findings.checked: The half-chord is 4 cm. Pythagoras gives distances 3 cm and √153 cm=3√17 cm. Both configurations are possible: each proposed centre separation lies strictly between the difference and sum of the radii.
findings.assumptions: Pythagoras and exact square-root notation are prior knowledge, supported by the separate course booklets. The common-chord theorem is available by the end of this topic.

repair.proposal: After p17-q6-block, optionally ask: “Two intersecting circles have radii 5 cm and 13 cm and a common chord 8 cm long. Find the distance between their centres when the centres are (a) on opposite sides of the chord and (b) on the same side. Explain.” Expected answers: (a) 3+3√17 cm; (b) 3√17−3 cm. Both centres lie on the chord’s perpendicular bisector.

findings.doneWhen: The optional task includes both configurations and requires an explanation of the sum or difference.

findings.finding: Generalise the angle relationships of a cyclic quadrilateral with parallel opposite sides.
findings.breakdown: Students combine cyclic opposite-angle sums with parallel-line co-interior angles.
findings.checked: For AB parallel to CD, A+D=180° and B+C=180°. Cyclicity gives A+C=180° and B+D=180°. Thus A=B=θ and C=D=180°−θ; all four angles are right angles exactly when θ=90°.
findings.assumptions: ABCD is a nondegenerate cyclic quadrilateral named in boundary order, with 0°<θ<180°. Parallel-line angle relationships are prior learning and are used in the existing exercise.

repair.proposal: After p27-r, optionally ask: “ABCD is a cyclic quadrilateral with AB parallel to CD. Let angle A=θ. Predict the other three angles, then justify your prediction. Under what condition is ABCD a rectangle?” Expected answer: B=θ, C=D=180°−θ; it is a rectangle exactly when θ=90°.

findings.doneWhen: Students justify the symbolic angles using both taught relationships.

findings.finding: Vary the external secant length while fixing the tangent length to expose the external-times-whole product.
findings.breakdown: The existing questions vary several givens together. This run isolates how whole and internal secant lengths change.
findings.checked: With tangent length 12 cm, whole length is 144/e and internal length is 144/e−e. The proposed external lengths are positive and less than 12 cm, so every internal length is positive. All numerical answers are correct.
findings.assumptions: Students use the tangent–secant product rule and linear-equation solving already available in this topic.

repair.proposal: After p33-q2-k, optionally add: “A tangent is 12 cm long. A secant from the same external point has external length e and internal length x. Predict how the whole secant and x change as e increases, then find both for e=3, 4, 6 and 8 cm. Explain using e(e+x)=144.” Expected whole/internal lengths: (48,45), (36,32), (24,18), (18,10) cm; both decrease. Follow with: “A tangent is 10 cm and the external secant is 4 cm. Find the whole and internal lengths.” Expected: 25 cm and 21 cm. Only e varies in the run; tangent length stays fixed.

findings.doneWhen: The run includes prediction, four calculations varying one given, an explanation and an unpatterned follow-up.

findings.finding: Generalise the incircle tangent-length equations into formulas and triangle inequalities.
findings.breakdown: Students return to the three-equation structure in question 8 and explain the meaning of positive tangent lengths.
findings.checked: Writing RB=RC=r, PA=PC=p and QA=QB=q gives r+q=a, r+p=b and p+q=c. Solving yields the proposed formulas, and their positivity gives exactly the three strict triangle inequalities.
findings.assumptions: PQR is a nondegenerate triangle with its incircle. Equal tangents and simultaneous-equation solving are available by this point.

repair.proposal: After p43-q8, optionally ask: “In triangle PQR, write RQ=a, PR=b and PQ=c. The incircle touches these sides at B, C and A respectively. Find RB, PA and QA in terms of a, b and c. Explain what their positivity tells you about the side lengths.” Expected answer: RB=(a+b−c)/2, PA=(b+c−a)/2, QA=(a+c−b)/2. Positivity gives a+b>c, b+c>a and a+c>b.

findings.doneWhen: Students derive the formulas from equal tangents and connect positivity to all three triangle inequalities.
